topic: Linear Transformations and Matrices: The Geometry of Change

sections.title: Prerequisites & The Intuitive Leap (0:00-0:45)
sections.content: Briefly recall vectors as arrows in a 2D plane (x, y). Introduce a 'Linear Transformation' as a function that moves the grid while keeping lines straight, parallel, and the origin fixed.
sections.example: Visualize a rubber grid being stretched or rotated like a piece of spandex fabric.

sections.title: Defining the Basis Vectors (0:45-1:45)
sections.content: Explain that any transformation is fully defined by where the unit basis vectors, î (1,0) and ĵ (0,1), land. This is the 'DNA' of the transformation.
sections.example: Show î moving to (2, -1) and ĵ moving to (0, 2) on an animated coordinate plane.

sections.title: The Matrix Representation (1:45-3:00)
sections.content: Introduce the 2x2 matrix as a compact notation to store these new coordinates of î and ĵ. Column 1 is where î lands; Column 2 is where ĵ lands.
sections.example: Using the previous example, construct the matrix [[2, 0], [-1, 2]]. Show how multiplying a general vector [x, y] by this matrix yields the new position.

sections.title: Application: The Game Character Transformation (3:00-4:15)
sections.content: Apply the matrix logic to a 2D character (e.g., a fox). If we want to flip the fox horizontally, we adjust the basis vectors and update the matrix.
sections.example: A 'Shear' transformation matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]] applied to an animated fox, showing the fox leaning sideways while maintaining its feet on the ground.

sections.title: Summary & Synthesis (4:15-5:00)
sections.content: Conclude that matrices are not just grids of numbers, but 'instruction manuals' for space. Recap: Transformation = Matrix x Vector.
sections.example: A quick montage: A rotation matrix spinning a star, followed by a scaling matrix making a cube grow and shrink.
